name: Vancouver
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Vancouver: real estate ownership, mining and trade diligence, asset tracing and BC litigation support.
hero_lede: Vancouver is Canada's Pacific gateway, with the country's busiest port, a junior mining capital and a property market shaped by international capital. TDSC scopes investigative consulting from Nashville for matters touching the city, coordinating BC-licensed investigators and the client's counsel where local work is required.
intro: Vancouver is the largest city in British Columbia, with 662,248 residents in the 2021 census, about a quarter of the Metro Vancouver region. It is Canada's main gateway to Asia-Pacific trade: its port moves bulk commodities, containers and autos, and Vancouver International Airport has extensive transpacific links. The city is a centre for resource company headquarters, particularly in mining and exploration, and for the financing, legal and engineering services that support them. Technology, film and television production, tourism, construction and real estate are major employers, and the British Columbia Securities Commission, provincial courts and many national law and accounting firms are based downtown.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Vancouver because international capital, commodities and property meet there. The provincial inquiry led by Justice Austin Cullen, which reported in 2022, examined how illicit funds moved through casinos, real estate and other sectors in British Columbia, and earlier provincial reviews highlighted anonymous property ownership. Investors in exploration companies need to understand promoters and related-party dealings; traders and shippers using the port need assurance about counterparties; and creditors pursuing recovery need to see through nominee and corporate property ownership. British Columbia's Land Owner Transparency Registry and its provincial licensing rules for investigators shape how this work is done.

matters.title: Real estate beneficial ownership
matters.text: Vancouver property has often been held through corporations, trusts and nominees. We combine land title records, Land Owner Transparency Registry reports, corporate filings and litigation to identify the people likely to stand behind a property and state the strength of each attribution for lenders, litigants and acquirers.

matters.title: Mining and exploration promoter diligence
matters.text: Many exploration companies are managed from Vancouver and hold projects abroad. We review management and promoter histories, securities regulatory actions, related-party transactions and litigation, and extend research to the countries where projects sit, before investment, financing or joint ventures.

matters.title: Port and trade counterparties
matters.text: Importers, exporters, freight forwarders and customs brokers using the Port of Vancouver can be used for misdeclaration or trade-based money laundering. We test ownership, operating substance, related entities in Asia and elsewhere, and regulatory and litigation history before clients finance or contract with them.

matters.title: Asset tracing for BC recovery
matters.text: Creditors enforcing judgments or awards against Vancouver-based debtors need to see through corporate, trust and family ownership of property and businesses. We map assets from public records so BC counsel can plan examinations in aid of execution, preservation orders and other enforcement steps.

matters.title: Securities and investment fraud support
matters.text: Investors who have lost money through Vancouver-managed issuers or private placements need facts about the people and entities involved. We assemble corporate histories, BC Securities Commission decisions, court records and fund flows from documents counsel can lawfully obtain, to support civil claims or regulatory complaints.

local_context.title: Courts sitting in Vancouver
local_context.text: The Supreme Court of British Columbia, the province's superior trial court, hears major commercial litigation, insolvency and enforcement matters at the Vancouver Law Courts, and the Court of Appeal for British Columbia also sits there. Federal matters such as maritime claims and intellectual property can be heard by the Federal Court, which sits in Vancouver. BC court decisions are widely published, but file access depends on the court registry and the type of proceeding; counsel decides the forum and we tailor research to its rules.

local_context.title: Land Owner Transparency Registry
local_context.text: British Columbia's Land Owner Transparency Act came into force on 30 November 2020, creating a registry operated by the Land Title and Survey Authority. Corporations, trustees and partnerships that hold land must report individuals with indirect interests, including holders of 10 percent or more of shares or votes. The public can search limited details such as name, citizenship and city of residence, while sensitive data is available only to authorities. This sits alongside the land title register, making Vancouver property ownership more traceable than in most Canadian cities.

local_context.title: Money laundering inquiry and reforms
local_context.text: The Commission of Inquiry into Money Laundering in British Columbia, led by Justice Austin Cullen, was established in 2019 and delivered its final report in June 2022. It examined the so-called Vancouver Model linking underground banking, casinos and real estate and criticised regulatory and federal enforcement failures. The provincial government publishes related anti-money laundering reports. For investigators, the inquiry's evidence and reports are a valuable reference on typologies and on the history of particular sectors.

local_context.title: BC investigator licensing and registries
local_context.text: Private investigators in British Columbia are licensed by the province under its security services legislation, and a licence from another province does not authorise work in BC, so any Vancouver fieldwork is carried out by BC-licensed investigators. Provincial companies are registered with BC Registries, and the British Columbia Securities Commission, headquartered in Vancouver, publishes enforcement decisions and filings that are central to research on local issuers and promoters.

tdsc_approach: TDSC has no office in Vancouver and works on Vancouver matters from Nashville. We agree the purpose with the client and its BC counsel first, whether a property or lending transaction, a mining investment, a trade relationship or the recovery of a judgment, and scope the work to it. Desk research draws on land title and Land Owner Transparency Registry searches, BC Registries filings, BC Securities Commission decisions, BC and federal court records, and Chinese-language and other media where relevant. Any surveillance or local enquiries are carried out by BC-licensed investigators within provincial privacy law. Reports separate confirmed facts from inferences and state confidence levels.

faqs.q: Can we find who really owns a Vancouver property?
faqs.a: Often more readily than elsewhere in Canada. The land title register shows the registered owner, and since 2020 the Land Owner Transparency Registry has required corporations, trusts and partnerships holding BC land to report individuals with indirect interests. Public searches show limited details. We combine these with corporate, litigation and media sources to confirm who is likely in control.

faqs.q: Does an investigator need a BC licence to work in Vancouver?
faqs.a: Yes. Private investigators are licensed provincially in British Columbia, and licences from other provinces or US states do not authorise work there. TDSC does not hold a BC licence. Where surveillance, interviews or other local enquiries are needed, we coordinate BC-licensed investigators and plan the work with the client's counsel.

faqs.q: How do you assess a Vancouver-managed mining company?
faqs.a: We review the issuer's filings and the BC Securities Commission's decisions, management and promoter histories, related-party dealings, litigation and media. Because projects are often abroad, we extend research to registries and courts where the assets sit, coordinating local professionals where needed, to test whether the company's account of its project and people holds up.

faqs.q: Where are commercial disputes heard in Vancouver?
faqs.a: Major commercial cases are heard by the Supreme Court of British Columbia at the Vancouver Law Courts, with appeals to the Court of Appeal for British Columbia. Maritime and certain federal matters may go to the Federal Court. Many cross-border contracts also choose arbitration seated in Vancouver. Counsel decides the forum.

faqs.q: Is the Cullen Commission relevant to due diligence today?
faqs.a: It can be. The inquiry's evidence and 2022 final report describe typologies involving casinos, real estate, underground banking and luxury goods in British Columbia, and they name sectors and practices that attracted scrutiny. We use such public material as context when assessing counterparties, while relying on current records for any conclusion about a particular person or company.
